title: Egg Size to Grams Converter 2026 — White, Yolk & Edible Weight
description: Convert egg sizes to grams of white, yolk and edible total. USDA-based standards: Large=57g, XL=64g. Free egg weight calculator for baking and cooking.
seoKeywords: how many grams in a large egg
how many grams is an egg white
intro:
You open a macaron recipe that calls for 90 g of egg whites. You look at your carton of large eggs and wonder: how many do I crack? That moment of doubt — familiar to home bakers and professional pastry chefs alike — is exactly what this calculator solves.

Egg sizes follow USDA standards based on minimum weight per dozen: Small ≈ 43 g, Medium ≈ 50 g, Large ≈ 57 g, Extra Large ≈ 64 g, and Jumbo ≈ 71 g (all weights include the shell). Most US and international recipes assume a Large egg when they say 'one egg' without specifying size.

Inside each egg, weight is distributed in stable proportions regardless of size: the shell accounts for about 9% of total weight, the white for 58%, and the yolk for 31% — figures based on USDA FoodData Central data (SR Legacy #01123). A Large egg of 57 g yields roughly 52 g edible: about 33 g of white and 18 g of yolk.

This calculator gives you the answer instantly: choose the size and number of eggs, and get grams of white, yolk, and total edible weight. No scale needed to get started, though for precision baking — macarons, soufflés, Italian meringue — always weigh directly.
keyTakeaway: **White ≈ 58% · Yolk ≈ 31% · Shell ≈ 9%** of whole egg weight — one Large egg (57 g) yields ~33 g of white and ~18 g of yolk.
useCases: Recipe calls for 90 g egg whites for French macarons: with Large eggs (~33 g white each) you need 3 eggs (99 g) — the calculator confirms exactly how much you get and how much is left over.
A European recipe specifies '4 Medium eggs' but you only have Extra Large: the calculator shows that 3 XL eggs provide almost the same total edible weight, saving you an egg.
Scaling a pastry recipe from 12 to 36 servings: instead of tripling the egg count, convert to grams (3 × 33 g = 99 g white) and weigh directly for consistent results.

Following a high-protein meal plan where your nutritionist specified 'white equivalent to 2 large eggs per day': the calculator confirms that is ~66 g, useful if buying cartons of pasteurized liquid whites.

explanation:
## How it works

The calculator uses the midpoint weight for each USDA size category, then applies stable physiological proportions:

```
Whole egg weight (with shell, USDA midpoints):
  Small (S)       ≈ 43 g
  Medium (M)      ≈ 50 g
  Large (L)       ≈ 57 g
  Extra Large (XL)≈ 64 g
  Jumbo (J)       ≈ 71 g

Proportions (USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy #01123):
  Shell  ≈ 9% of whole weight
  White  ≈ 58% of whole weight
  Yolk   ≈ 31% of whole weight

Formulas:
  White (g)       = whole_weight × 0.58 × count
  Yolk (g)        = whole_weight × 0.31 × count
  Edible (g)      = whole_weight × 0.91 × count
```

---

## Reference table

| USDA Size       | Whole weight (g) | White (g) | Yolk (g) | Edible (g) |
|-----------------|-----------------|-----------|----------|------------|
| Small (S)       | ~43             | ~25       | ~13      | ~39        |
| Medium (M)      | ~50             | ~29       | ~16      | ~46        |
| Large (L)       | ~57             | ~33       | ~18      | ~52        |
| Extra Large (XL)| ~64             | ~37       | ~20      | ~58        |
| Jumbo (J)       | ~71             | ~41       | ~22      | ~65        |

> Values are per single egg. For precision baking (macarons, soufflés), always weigh whites directly on a kitchen scale.

---

## Common mistakes

1. **Treating size labels as interchangeable:** A Medium egg (50 g) provides 29 g of white; a Large (57 g) provides 33 g — a 14% difference that matters in delicate emulsions and meringues.

2. **Ignoring the shell weight:** ~9% of the whole egg is shell. A 57 g egg yields only ~52 g edible. Forgetting this causes shortfalls when scaling large batches.

3. **Mixing liquid pasteurized whites with fresh white weights:** Most commercial cartons specify the equivalent (e.g., '3 tablespoons = 1 large egg white'). Use that label figure, not a fresh egg calculation.

4. **Scaling by unit count instead of weight:** When a recipe triples, cracking 9 instead of 3 eggs can introduce ±30 g variation if sizes vary. Convert to grams, weigh, and eliminate uncertainty.

faq.q: How many grams is a large egg?
faq.a: A USDA Large egg weighs approximately 57 grams with the shell. The edible portion (white + yolk) is about 52 grams: roughly 33 g of white and 18 g of yolk. The shell accounts for about 5 g (~9% of total weight). Most American and many international recipes use Large as the default when no size is specified.

faq.q: How much does an egg white weigh in grams?
faq.a: Egg white weight depends on the egg size. Based on USDA data (white ≈ 58% of whole egg weight): Small ≈ 25 g, Medium ≈ 29 g, Large ≈ 33 g, Extra Large ≈ 37 g, Jumbo ≈ 41 g. For precision recipes like macarons or Italian meringue, always weigh whites on a kitchen scale rather than relying on egg count alone.

faq.q: How much does an egg yolk weigh?
faq.a: Yolk weight is approximately 31% of the whole egg's weight (USDA FoodData Central). For common sizes: Medium yolk ≈ 16 g, Large yolk ≈ 18 g, Extra Large yolk ≈ 20 g, Jumbo yolk ≈ 22 g. The yolk's proportional share stays consistent across sizes, so switching sizes primarily changes absolute grams, not ratios.

faq.q: How do I substitute Medium eggs for Large eggs in a recipe?
faq.a: Match the total edible weight, not the unit count. Four Large eggs provide about 4 × 52 g = 208 g edible. Medium eggs yield ~46 g edible each, so you need 208 ÷ 46 ≈ 4.5 → use 5 Medium eggs. For casual cooking (scrambled eggs, frittata) one extra egg rarely matters; for technical baking (chiffon cake, soufflé, custard) the extra mass changes moisture balance and structure.

faq.q: How many grams of egg white do I need for French macarons?
faq.a: Classic French macaron recipes typically call for 90–100 g of aged egg whites for a standard batch of 30–36 shells. With Large eggs (~33 g white each), that's 3 eggs (99 g). With Medium eggs (~29 g each), you'd need 4 eggs (116 g, with ~16–26 g leftover to set aside). Most pastry chefs recommend weighing, not counting, and aging the whites uncovered in the fridge for 24–48 hours before use.

faq.q: Does egg freshness affect the weight or white-to-yolk ratio?
faq.a: Egg weight decreases slightly over time as moisture evaporates through the porous shell — an egg can lose 2–4 g over its shelf life. The white-to-yolk ratio stays essentially constant in terms of mass, but the texture changes: older eggs have more liquid white (the thick albumen converts to thin albumen), which can actually be useful for macarons because the whites flow more easily without the stringy thick white. For precision baking, always check the weight, not just the size printed on the carton.

faq.q: How do I convert eggs to grams of liquid pasteurized egg white?
faq.a: Most commercial cartons of pasteurized liquid egg whites indicate on the label how much equals one whole egg white (typically 30–35 ml or 30–35 g per large egg white). Use that stated equivalent rather than the fresh-egg weight, because pasteurized liquid whites may differ slightly in density. If the label is unclear, 33 g (Large) is a reliable starting point, but weigh and taste-check before committing to a full batch.

faq.q: How do USDA egg sizes compare to European egg sizes?
faq.a: The European Union uses a different grading system: S (< 53 g), M (53–63 g), L (63–73 g), XL (> 73 g). A European 'L' (63–73 g) is heavier than a USDA 'Large' (≈ 57 g) and closer to a USDA Extra Large. When following a European recipe that calls for 'L' eggs, use USDA Extra Large or Jumbo for the closest match. When in doubt, the safest approach is to convert the recipe to grams rather than unit count.

faq.q: What are the calories in egg white vs. egg yolk?
faq.a: According to USDA FoodData Central: egg white provides about 52 kcal per 100 g (mostly protein, virtually no fat, no cholesterol). Egg yolk is much more calorie-dense at about 322 kcal per 100 g, with ~27% fat and significant cholesterol (~1,100 mg/100 g). A whole Large egg (edible portion, ~52 g) contains about 72–75 kcal total. Knowing the exact gram weight of whites and yolks — what this calculator provides — makes it straightforward to track macros for either component.

faq.q: How much does a dozen eggs weigh?
faq.a: Per USDA minimum weight standards per dozen: Small ≈ 510 g, Medium ≈ 595 g, Large ≈ 680 g, Extra Large ≈ 765 g, Jumbo ≈ 850 g. These are minimum weights, so actual cartons may be slightly heavier. The per-egg averages used in this calculator (43 g, 50 g, 57 g, 64 g, 71 g) are derived by dividing the midpoint of each USDA dozen-weight band by 12.
